title: Gemini Prompting in Practice
summary: This intermediate module enables learners to write, evaluate, and revise structured prompts for Gemini. After completing it, learners can turn a loosely stated task into a prompt with explicit instructions, relevant context, a defined output format, and examples when needed.
objectives: Write a Gemini prompt that states the task, relevant context, output format, and success criteria explicitly.
Use examples to demonstrate a desired response pattern when instructions alone are insufficient.
Break a complex prompting task into smaller steps.
Evaluate a response against stated criteria and revise the prompt to address a specific problem.

paragraphs: The source record associated with content/modules/google-gemini-practice/gemini-prompting-in-practice.json was listed as an unregistered publisher and had never been verified. It has been replaced by Google's official Prompt design strategies documentation.

This correction affects the source URL, publisher attribution, verification date, and the support for the prompting guidance in this module. The instructional scope remains focused on practical prompt construction and revision.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate module. It assumes that you can already write a basic natural-language prompt and inspect the resulting response. It does not assume programming knowledge or knowledge of advanced model configuration.

The goal is to move beyond a one-line request. You will learn to express the task, supply relevant context, define the expected form of the response, and revise the prompt when the response does not satisfy your criteria.

sections.title: Make the task explicit
paragraphs: Begin by stating what Gemini should do. Prefer a direct instruction such as asking it to summarize, compare, classify, explain, or transform supplied material. Include the intended audience or purpose when that information changes what a useful response looks like.

State observable success criteria rather than relying on a vague request for a better response. Criteria can identify the required coverage, the desired degree of detail, or constraints the response must follow.

Define the output format when structure matters. For example, request a short paragraph followed by three questions if that is the form you need. A format instruction gives you a concrete feature to check in the response.

sections.title: Supply relevant context
paragraphs: Include information that Gemini needs in order to complete the task. Relevant context may include source text, definitions, audience needs, or boundaries on what material the response should use.

Separate instructions from supplied material so their roles are clear. Introduce the material with plain labels such as Instructions and Source text. This helps distinguish what Gemini should do from the content it should process.
Do not add unrelated context merely to make the prompt longer. Each included detail should help determine the task, the expected response, or the criteria used to evaluate it.

sections.title: Use examples when a pattern is hard to describe
paragraphs: Examples can demonstrate the relationship between an input and the response you want. They are useful when tone, classification boundaries, or formatting rules would be difficult to communicate with instructions alone.
Keep examples consistent with one another and with the written instructions. If an example contradicts a rule, the prompt presents competing signals and becomes harder to evaluate.
An example should demonstrate the desired pattern rather than provide unrelated content. After the examples, present the new input clearly so it is distinguishable from the demonstrations.

sections.title: Divide complex work into smaller steps
paragraphs: When a task contains several distinct operations, separate them into ordered steps. For example, a prompt can first ask for the important claims in supplied text and then ask for a summary based on those claims.
Breaking work into steps makes each requirement easier to inspect. It also helps you identify which instruction needs revision when the final response does not meet the stated criteria.
A step should contribute directly to the requested result. Remove steps that do not affect the final output or its evaluation.

sections.title: Evaluate and revise
paragraphs: Evaluate the response against the criteria written in the prompt. Check whether it performed the requested task, used the relevant context, followed the output format, and matched any demonstrated pattern.

If the response fails a criterion, revise the part of the prompt connected to that failure. Clarify an ambiguous instruction, add missing context, correct an inconsistent example, or make the required format more explicit.
Change one meaningful part at a time when diagnosing a problem. Compare the next response with the same criteria so you can determine whether the revision addressed the identified issue.
sections.callout: A practical prompt includes enough information to perform and evaluate the task, not merely more words.

sections.title: A reusable prompting workflow
paragraphs: First, write a direct task instruction. Second, add only the context needed for that task. Third, state the required output format and success criteria. Fourth, add consistent examples if the desired pattern remains difficult to describe. Fifth, divide the work into steps if it contains multiple operations.
After receiving a response, compare it with the success criteria. Identify one specific failure, revise the corresponding part of the prompt, and evaluate the next response using the same criteria.
Following this workflow enables you to turn an underspecified request into a prompt whose instructions and results can be inspected systematically.

questions.prompt: Which prompt most clearly defines both a task and an output format?
choices: Write something useful about the source text.
Summarize the supplied source text for a general audience in one paragraph, followed by three review questions.
questions.explanation: The correct prompt states the task, identifies the audience, and specifies a response format that can be checked.

questions.prompt: What should you do when using examples to demonstrate a desired response pattern?
choices: Make the examples inconsistent so that Gemini can choose among them.
Use examples only as unrelated background information.
Keep the examples consistent with one another and with the written instructions.
Replace every task instruction with an example.
questions.explanation: The module states that examples should be consistent with each other and with the written instructions so they demonstrate one clear pattern.

questions.prompt: How should you handle a task containing several distinct operations?
choices: Combine every operation into one vague instruction.
Separate the operations into ordered steps.
questions.explanation: The module recommends separating distinct operations into ordered steps so each requirement is easier to perform and inspect.

questions.prompt: A response uses the source text correctly but ignores the requested response structure. Which revision best follows the module's workflow?
choices: Make the required output format more explicit.
questions.explanation: The failure concerns structure, so the revision should clarify the output-format instruction connected to that failure.
